title: Psalms
subtitle: Israel's songs and prayers, from the cry for help to the last Praise the LORD
lead: The book of Psalms is a collection of 150 songs and prayers. Some cry to God for help in sickness, danger or guilt. Some thank him for a rescue. Some praise him as the maker of the world and the king of Israel. Some teach, like the opening psalm, which sets two paths before the reader: the way of the person who delights in the LORD's law, and the way of the wicked. Some were sung at the crowning of Judah's kings, some by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the festivals, some by exiles far from home. The Hebrew name of the book is Tehillim, "praises"; the English name comes from the Greek psalmoi, "songs sung to strings."

The psalms speak to God as often as they speak about him. That is why Jews and Christians have prayed them for more than two thousand years, in the temple and the synagogue, in monasteries that sing all 150 every week, in Protestant hymnals and in private prayer. The collection is arranged in five books (1–41, 42–72, 73–89, 90–106, 107–150), each ending with a blessing of God, perhaps on the pattern of the five books of Moses. It moves, on the whole, from lament to praise: the cries for help gather in the first half, and the book ends with a run of psalms that each begin and end with "Praise the LORD!" (146–150). Seventy-three psalms are headed "of David" in the Hebrew, and many headings name a tune, an instrument or a moment in David's life. The New Testament quotes the Psalms more than any other book of the Old Testament, reading them above all as words about and by the Messiah.
facts: Many. The titles name David (73 psalms in the Hebrew), Asaph (12), the sons of Korah (11), Solomon (2), Moses (Psalm 90), Heman and Ethan (88, 89); about a third have no name. The phrase translated "of David" (le-david) can mean "by David," "for David" or "belonging to the David collection" (see 3:0). Jewish tradition says David gathered the psalms of ten elders (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a). Most scholars think many singers and editors wrote and collected them over several centuries.

From the time of David (about 1000 BC) on the traditional view, or from the kings of Judah (900s–500s BC) for the oldest royal and temple psalms on most critical views, down to after the exile for psalms like 126 and 137. Most scholars think the five-book Psalter took its final shape in the Persian or early Greek period (400s–200s BC); the Dead Sea Scrolls show that the order of the last third was still not fixed everywhere in the first century BC.

Israel's worship: the temple in Jerusalem on Mount Zion, its festivals and sacrifices, its Levite singers (1 Chronicles 16:4–7; 25:1–7), the king's court, the sickbed and the private room, and later the synagogue and the household of exiles.

Hebrew poetry: laments (individual and communal), hymns of praise, songs of thanksgiving, royal psalms, songs of Zion, wisdom and law psalms, songs of trust, and liturgies for entering the temple (15; 24). Lines go in pairs or threes that echo each other (parallelism); nine psalms are acrostics, their lines beginning with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order (9–10, 25, 34, 37, 111, 112, 119, 145).

150 psalms, 2,461 verses in English numbering, not counting the titles (the Hebrew counts most titles as verse 1, so its verse numbers often run one higher). The Greek and Latin number the psalms differently, usually one lower from Psalm 10 to Psalm 147. The Greek Bible adds Psalm 151.

Book I: 1–41. Book II: 42–72 (ending "Here end the prayers of David son of Jesse," 72:20). Book III: 73–89. Book IV: 90–106. Book V: 107–150. Each book closes with a blessing of God (41:13; 72:18–19; 89:52; 106:48); Psalm 150 closes the whole.

Hebrew and English: 1–150. Greek and Latin (used in Catholic and Orthodox liturgy and older Catholic Bibles): Greek 9 = Hebrew 9–10; Greek 10–112 = Hebrew 11–113; Greek 113 = Hebrew 114–115; Greek 114–115 = Hebrew 116; Greek 116–145 = Hebrew 117–146; Greek 146–147 = Hebrew 147; 148–150 are the same. Each chapter page gives the Greek number.

audience.to: Israel at worship, in two layers. Each psalm was first sung or prayed by someone in a particular setting: a king before battle or at his crowning, a sick or accused person at the temple, a choir of Levites at a festival, pilgrims on the road to Jerusalem, a congregation after defeat or exile. The collected book of 150 psalms was made for a later audience: Jews of the Second Temple period, after the return from Babylon (from the 500s BC on), who had no king of David's line on the throne, who gathered at the rebuilt temple and in their homes and later their synagogues, and who prayed these words together and alone.
audience.why: To give Israel words to speak to God: words for praise, thanks, confession, trust, protest and grief, all said in the presence of the LORD and shaped for public and private use. Collected and arranged, the psalms also teach. Psalm 1 opens the book as a book of instruction to be read and "murmured" day and night; Psalm 2 sets God's anointed king at its center; the five books echo the five books of Moses. For readers after the exile, the royal psalms kept alive God's promise to David (89; 132) and the hope of a coming anointed king, and the laments gave them a way to bring loss and doubt to God without leaving him. Knowing these two layers changes the reading: a psalm may be one person's cry in one crisis, and at the same time a prayer the whole people learned to pray in theirs.
views: On the traditional view the titles tell the first setting: David composed many psalms out of the events of his life (3; 51; 57) and organized the temple singers who sang them (1 Chronicles 16:7; 25:1). The audience then widens from David's own prayer to all Israel singing it.

Since Hermann Gunkel and Sigmund Mowinckel most scholars read the psalms by type and setting in Israel's worship: hymns for festivals, laments for days of fasting, thanksgivings sung with a thank offering, royal psalms for the king's coronation and his wars. Mowinckel proposed a yearly festival at which the LORD was hailed as king (47; 93; 95–99); this remains debated.

Many recent scholars (Brevard Childs, Gerald Wilson and others) read the Psalter as a book shaped by its editors for reading and meditation after the exile. They see its order as meaningful: the failure of David's kingdom by the end of Book III (89), the answer "the LORD is king" in Book IV (93; 95–99), and the turn to praise in Book V.

Scholars debate how far the "I" of the laments is one person and how far it speaks for the people or the king. Many think personal prayers were adapted for the congregation, so that later Israel prayed "I" as a people.

authorship: The titles name David as author of 73 psalms in the Hebrew (and more in the Greek), and the New Testament quotes several as his (Mark 12:36; Acts 2:25; Acts 4:25; Romans 4:6). Jewish tradition says David wrote the book with the help of ten elders, among them Adam, Melchizedek, Abraham, Moses, Heman, Jeduthun, Asaph and the three sons of Korah (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a). Chronicles presents David as the organizer of the temple singers (1 Chronicles 16:4–7; 1 Chronicles 25:1–7). On this view the titles are reliable, and David composed many psalms out of the events of his life, while others were written by the singers he appointed and by later poets such as Moses (90) and Solomon (72; 127).

The Hebrew le-david can mean "by David," but also "for David," "about David," "in the manner of David" or "belonging to the David collection." Some psalms headed "of David" mention the temple (5:7; 27:4) or the exile (69:35–36), which leads many readers, including some conservative ones, to think the phrase does not always claim authorship.

Most scholars think the titles were added by editors, perhaps in the Persian period, and that the psalms come from many singers over many centuries: some from the time of the monarchy (the royal psalms, 2; 18; 45; 72; 110), some from temple choirs (Asaph, Korah), some from the exile and after (74; 79; 126; 137). Hermann Gunkel sorted them by type and setting; Sigmund Mowinckel tied many to festivals in the temple. Brevard Childs argued that the event titles (such as 3:0 and 51:0) are early interpretations, linking the psalms with stories in Samuel.

Gerald Wilson and others have studied the shaping of the whole: royal psalms at the seams of the five books (2; 72; 89), the collapse of David's kingdom lamented in 89, the answer "the LORD is king" in Book IV (93–99), and the turn to praise in Book V. On this view the book's final editors, not only its poets, are its authors.

lenses.name: Titles as history
lenses.desc: Many Jewish and Christian readers take the psalm titles as reliable notes about who wrote each psalm and when: David in the cave, David after Bathsheba, the sons of Korah at the temple. The New Testament quotes several psalms as David's (Mark 12:36; Acts 2:25; Romans 4:6).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read the titles as later notes by the collectors, and sort the psalms by type (laments, hymns, thanksgivings, royal and wisdom psalms) and by setting in Israel's worship. They date the collection over centuries, with the five-book shape finished after the exile.

lenses.name: In worship
lenses.desc: How each psalm was sung and prayed: in the temple, in the synagogue and the Jewish prayer book, in the church's daily prayer, liturgy and hymns, and in private prayer.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The Talmud, the Midrash on Psalms (Midrash Tehillim), the Targum and the medieval commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak), and the psalms' place in Jewish prayer.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: How the New Testament and the church read the psalms as prayers of Christ and of his people, from the fathers (Augustine, Athanasius, Cassiodorus) to Luther, Calvin and today.

sections.b:
The text page beside each psalm can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English Translation

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. The Psalms are poetry: the Plain English Translation keeps one verse per line, marks the poetic lines with slashes, and tries to keep parallel lines parallel and short. Where the Hebrew is uncertain, the Plain English Translation gives the most likely sense and a note gives the alternatives.

Titles and numbers

A psalm's title (its heading) is printed as verse 0, as in most English Bibles; Hebrew Bibles count it as verse 1, so their verse numbers often run one higher (see 3:0). The Greek and Latin number most psalms one lower than the Hebrew; each psalm page gives its Greek number (see "Numbering" below).

Key terms

YHWH is "the LORD" (see 1:2). Ashrei is "Happy" (1:1). Hesed is "loyal love" (5:7). Torah is "law" (1:2). Selah is kept as it is (3:2), and so are maskil, miktam and shiggaion (7:0; 16:0). She'ol is "Sheol," the world of the dead (6:5). Lamnatseach is "For the music director" (4:0). Hallelu-yah is "Praise the LORD!"

sections.h: The five books and the shape of the Psalter
sections.b:
The Psalter is divided into five books, each closed by a short blessing of God: Book I (1–41) ends at 41:13, Book II (42–72) at 72:18–19 with the note "Here end the prayers of David son of Jesse" (72:20), Book III (73–89) at 89:52, Book IV (90–106) at 106:48, and Book V (107–150) with the whole of Psalm 150. The Midrash on Psalms compares the five books with the five books of Moses.

Psalms 1 and 2 form the gateway: the LORD's teaching and the LORD's king. Books I and II are mostly psalms of David, largely laments. Book III, with psalms of Asaph and Korah, darkens: the temple destroyed (74; 79), the covenant with David apparently broken (89). Book IV answers with Moses (90) and the cry "The LORD is king" (93; 95–99). Book V gathers praise and pilgrimage: the Hallel (113–118), the great torah psalm (119), the Songs of Ascents (120–134), a last group of David psalms (138–145) and the closing Hallelujahs (146–150). Many scholars read this shape as a story from lament to praise and from human kingship to God's kingship; others think the arrangement is looser.

sections.h: Titles, music and the Hebrew poetry
sections.b:
Of the 150 psalms, 116 have a title in the Hebrew. Titles name an author or collection (David, Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses, Heman, Ethan), a kind of song ("a psalm," "a song," "a prayer," "a maskil"), musical directions ("for the music director," "with stringed instruments"), tunes ("on muth-labben," 9:0; "on 'The Doe of the Dawn,'" 22:0) and sometimes an event in David's life (3:0; 51:0). The meaning of many words was already lost when the Greek translation was made. See the topics on psalm titles and music.

Hebrew poetry has no rhyme and no strict meter. Its basic unit is a line of two or three parts that echo each other (parallelism): the second may repeat the first in other words ("Why do the nations gather in an uproar, / and the peoples murmur over empty plans?" 2:1), sharpen it, contrast with it (1:6), or carry it further. Nine psalms are alphabet poems (acrostics), each line or stanza beginning with the next Hebrew letter: 9–10, 25, 34, 37, 111, 112, 119 and 145. The chapter pages name the letters.

The Hebrew and the Greek divide some psalms differently. The Greek (followed by the Latin Vulgate, by Catholic and Orthodox liturgy, and by older Catholic Bibles such as Douay-Rheims) counts Psalms 9 and 10 as one psalm, and Psalms 114 and 115 as one, but splits Psalm 116 into two and Psalm 147 into two. The result:

  • Hebrew 1–8 = Greek 1–8
  • Hebrew 9–10 = Greek 9
  • Hebrew 11–113 = Greek 10–112
  • Hebrew 114–115 = Greek 113
  • Hebrew 116 = Greek 114–115
  • Hebrew 117–146 = Greek 116–145
  • Hebrew 147 = Greek 146–147
  • Hebrew 148–150 = Greek 148–150

So the famous "Psalm 22" is Psalm 21 in an Orthodox prayer book, and "Psalm 51" is the Miserere, Psalm 50. Verse numbers also differ: Hebrew Bibles count most titles as verse 1. This site uses the Hebrew and English psalm numbers, English verse numbers, and the title as verse 0.

sections.h: The text: Hebrew, Greek, Qumran and the versions
sections.b:
The Plain English Translation follows the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), the oldest complete Hebrew Bible. The other witnesses are weighed in the variants:

  • The Old Greek (the Septuagint), translated in the 200s–100s BC, often reads differently and is quoted by the New Testament (2:9; 8:2; 16:10). Its Psalter adds Psalm 151 and has titles where the Hebrew has none.
  • The Dead Sea Scrolls. Psalms are the book found in the most copies: about forty scrolls from Qumran, Masada and Nahal Hever (as reported; Flint lists them). The Great Psalms Scroll (11QPs-a, first century AD) has psalms from Books IV and V in a different order, mixed with other poems: a longer Hebrew Psalm 151, the "Plea for Deliverance," a hymn to the Creator, and a prose note crediting David with 4,050 songs (contents as reported in Sanders' edition). Scholars debate whether it is another edition of the Psalter or a collection for worship. Most fragments of Books I–III agree closely with the Masoretic Text.
  • Later versions: the Syriac Peshitta, Jerome's two Latin Psalters (the Gallican, revised from the Greek and used in the Vulgate, and the Psalter iuxta Hebraeos, from the Hebrew) and the Aramaic Targum of Psalms.

For each part of the Psalms the variant notes say which witnesses were checked directly and which are given as reported. For Psalms 1–17 the list is on the page of Psalm 1: the Old Greek and the Gallican Psalter were checked directly on a polyglot page of Rahlfs' Greek text and the Vulgate; the Qumran fragments, the Targum, Jerome's Hebrew Psalter, Aquila and Symmachus are cited as reported.

The Hebrew Bible has 150 psalms, and so do Protestant Bibles. Greek manuscripts of the Psalter, among them Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Alexandrinus, add Psalm 151, headed "This psalm is ascribed to David, outside the number, when he fought Goliath alone." It tells how the youngest son, a shepherd who made a lyre, was chosen and anointed over his brothers and cut off the giant's head. The Orthodox churches accept it and read it in their Psalter; it is in the Syriac Bible and in the appendix of some Latin Bibles, but the Catholic Church does not count it as canonical, and Protestants do not. The Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a) has a longer Hebrew form in two parts (often called 151A and 151B), showing that the Greek was translated from a Hebrew original. Psalm 151 is not printed in this site's Plain English Translation; see the page on Psalm 151 among the books outside the 66.

sections.h: Praying the Psalms: Jews and Christians
sections.b:
The Levites sang a psalm for each weekday at the daily offering in the Second Temple (Mishnah Tamid 7:4; the Greek titles of 24, 48, 94 and 93 keep some of the days). The Hallel (113–118) was sung at the festivals and at Passover, and Jesus and his disciples "sang a hymn" after the Last Supper (Mark 14:26). In the synagogue and the Jewish prayer book the psalms frame the morning service (145–150), welcome the Sabbath (92; 95–99; 29), and are said for the sick, the dying and the dead; many Jews read the whole Psalter each week or month.

Christians have sung psalms from the beginning (1 Corinthians 14:26; Colossians 3:16). Monasteries recite all 150 each week (Rule of Benedict 18), the Roman Liturgy of the Hours spreads them over four weeks, and the Book of Common Prayer over a month. Reformed churches in Geneva and Scotland put them into metrical verse to sing (the Genevan Psalter of 1562; the Scottish Psalter of 1650), and some still sing only psalms. Athanasius wrote that while the rest of Scripture speaks to us, the Psalms speak for us; Bonhoeffer called the Psalter "the prayer book of the Bible," prayed by Christ and by his church.

Some psalms pray for God to punish enemies in harsh terms (35; 69; 109; 137:7–9; compare 5:10). Readers have handled them in different ways. Many scholars stress that they are prayers handed over to God, not acts of revenge, from people with no power, asking God the judge to act (compare Romans 12:19). Jewish tradition keeps them in the Psalter and in study, and reads their enemies as the enemies of God and of Israel. Christian readers have read them as prayers against sin and the devil (Augustine), as the words of Christ the judge (Bonhoeffer), as an honest cry of the oppressed (Brueggemann), or as words Christians may not pray after Jesus' command to love enemies (C. S. Lewis judged them wrong but instructive). The Roman Liturgy of the Hours since 1971 leaves out Psalms 58 [57], 83 [82] and 109 [108] (Greek numbers in brackets) and some verses of others; the Orthodox and many Protestant churches keep them all. See the box below and the chapter pages of 35, 69, 109 and 137.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the book that learns to stop asking 'how long?'
spec.body: My own reading: the question "how long?" runs through the Psalter's first half and then fades. It starts early (6:3; 13:1–2), returns at the darkest points (74:10; 79:5; 80:4; 89:46) and appears for the last time in Book IV, in Moses' prayer (90:13) and in 94:3. After that the question disappears, and Book V answers with the Songs of Ascents and the Hallelujahs. If the editors arranged the book as many scholars think, from lament to praise, the fading of this one question may be a thread they followed on purpose: the book does not answer "how long?" with a date but with the kingship of God (93–99). Scholars have traced the movement from lament to praise; following it through this particular question is my suggestion, and it rests on where the phrase happens to fall.

prompts: The tree by the water channels (1:3)

A single broad tree in full leaf and fruit stands beside narrow irrigation channels cut through a dry, golden plain. A man sits in its shade with an open scroll on his knees, his lips moving. Far off, on a windy hilltop threshing floor, figures toss grain into the air and the chaff blows away like smoke.


Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. traditions.q: Should churches sing only psalms in worship?
views: Divided. Reformed Presbyterian churches (the RPCNA and others), the Free Presbyterian Church of Scotland and the Free Church of Scotland (Continuing) hold to exclusive psalmody, as the Free Church of Scotland did until 2010: God has given his church its songbook, and only the inspired psalms, usually sung without instruments, belong in public worship (Westminster Confession 21.5 names 'singing of psalms'). Most other Reformed churches sing hymns too, as Calvin's Geneva sang the Ten Commandments and the Song of Simeon beside the psalms.
No. Luther wrote hymns and urged new songs of the gospel alongside the psalms, many of them psalm paraphrases ('A Mighty Fortress' on Psalm 46).
No. The psalms form the core of the Liturgy of the Hours and the responsorial psalm of the Mass, but hymns and canticles belong to the Church's worship too.
No. The whole Psalter is sung or said each month in the Book of Common Prayer, alongside canticles and hymns.
No. Charles and John Wesley wrote and published thousands of hymns, though they also sang psalm paraphrases.

traditions.q: Should the curse psalms be prayed in public worship?
views: The Liturgy of the Hours since 1971 omits Psalms 58 [57], 83 [82] and 109 [108] (Greek numbers in brackets) and certain verses of others, explaining that some passages are hard for the faithful; they remain Scripture and are read in study (General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours 131).
The whole Psalter is read in the services each week, curse psalms included; the enemies are commonly understood as the passions and the demons.
Psalm-singing churches sing all 150, reading the curses as prayers for God's justice and against his enemies, to be prayed in Christ, who is both savior and judge.
The 1662 Book of Common Prayer appoints all the psalms; some later Anglican prayer books and psalters mark verses that may be left out in public reading.

Opinions vary: many read them as honest prayers handed over to God, fulfilled in the judgment of Christ; some, following C. S. Lewis, see them as human anger God allowed to be recorded but not to be imitated.
